MSK-SKIN · WEEK 14 · LECTURE 4

The Spectrum of Eczema

Loretta S. Davis, MD · Full Lecture Companion · 53-slide course source

← Week 14Condensed FactoidHistologyAllergic contactCorticosteroidsAtopicEczema patterns
Big picture: Eczema is an itchy, spongiotic reaction pattern with diverse causes. First recognize its morphology and stage, then diagnose the trigger, and finally match therapy to the site, severity and risk of adverse effects.

1 · The eczema pattern

Eczema refers to a common, inflammatory, often intensely pruritic reaction pattern with many possible triggers. Margins tend to be poorly defined, though the lecturer cautions that this is not universal. The defining microscopic reaction is spongiosis—intercellular edema within the epidermis—which can expand into intraepidermal vesicles.

MUST KNOW · Eczema is a reaction pattern, not one etiology. Recognizing spongiosis and lesion age is the first task; identifying allergic, irritant, atopic or other triggers comes next.

Evolution over time

StageAppearancePathologic direction
AcuteOozing, vesiclesProminent epidermal spongiosis; vesiculation
SubacuteCrustingMixed active inflammation and early thickening
ChronicLichenification/thickened skinHyperkeratosis, acanthosis and reduced spongiosis

2 · Acute versus chronic eczematous histopathology

Acute spongiotic dermatitis

  • Normal stratum corneum
  • No acanthosis
  • Prominent epidermal spongiosis
  • Intraepidermal vesicles
  • Papillary dermal edema

Chronic eczematous dermatitis

  • Hyperkeratosis
  • Acanthosis
  • Only mild spongiosis
  • No vesicles
  • Thickened collagen with vertical streaking
Mechanism chain: pruritus → repeated scratching and rubbing → chronic epidermal thickening and accentuated skin lines (lichenification).

3 · Allergic contact eczema: type IV delayed hypersensitivity

Allergic contact eczema is an immune-mediated, T-cell memory phenomenon. First exposure sensitizes; on re-exposure, memory T cells recognize the allergen and generate eczema. The lecturer explicitly identifies this as a type IV hypersensitivity reaction. The distribution can trace the exposure surface, helping distinguish it from generalized atopic dermatitis.

Poison ivy and cross-exposure

Poison-ivy resin may be carried on fingernails, tools, pet fur and clothing. The slide explicitly states that blister fluid is not contagious. Mango skin is highlighted as a cross-reacting exposure. A superpotent topical corticosteroid is a lecture treatment example; when severe cases require oral corticosteroids, the lecture specifies a three-week course to avoid rebound from an inadequate course.

Important course-specific contrast: Oral corticosteroids are discouraged in the prior psoriasis lecture; this lecture discusses occasional longer oral courses for severe poison ivy. Do not generalize a single steroid rule across conditions.

Nickel and other allergens

Nickel occurs in earrings, jewelry, eyeglass frames, fasteners, buckles and tools. Distribution at sites of metal contact is a diagnostic clue. Lecturer emphasizes avoidance, with non-nickel materials such as selected stainless steel or gold. Common additional sensitizers include preservatives and fragrances; images also emphasize that some topical medicaments themselves can be offending exposures.

Patch testing

Delayed readings illustrated at 48 and 96 hours can establish allergy to specific contactants. Patch testing probes a type IV response; it is not the same as immediate skin-prick testing for IgE-mediated allergy.

4 · Topical corticosteroids: potency, vehicle and harm

Potency is a function of the molecule and the vehicle—not simply the number before the percent sign. The lecture contrasts 0.05% clobetasol (far stronger) with 2.5% hydrocortisone. In general, the lecturer orders vehicles ointment > cream > lotion > solution for potency/occlusion.

Skin/siteSlide guidanceExamples
Thick palm/sole or severe thick plaqueSuper-high potencyClobetasol (class I)
Trunk, extremities, atopic eczemaMedium/high potencyTriamcinolone (class IV in slides)
Face, groin, folds, childrenLow potencyHydrocortisone (class VI/VII)

Choose usable vehicles: solution, foam or shampoo for scalp; gel or lotion for hairy chest; avoid adding moisture/occlusion to already moist intertriginous sites when moisture is a driver. Patient acceptance influences adherence.

Adverse effects

Repeated use of strong topical steroids can cause skin atrophy and permanent striae: newer lesions are erythematous, older ones silvery. Other slide examples include perioral dermatitis, tinea incognito (fungal infection altered/masked by steroid), and possible systemic absorption with adrenal suppression. The lecturer recommends limited, flare-directed use rather than prolonged indiscriminate high-potency application.

5 · Irritant contact eczema: direct barrier injury

Unlike allergic contact eczema, irritant eczema does not require an immune sensitization problem. Harsh detergent, solvent, acid, excessive washing/sanitizer, urine/stool and saliva directly disrupt the skin barrier. The slide names dishpan hands, irritant diaper dermatitis, and lip-licker dermatitis.

Compare: Allergic = delayed type IV memory after sensitization, targeted allergen avoidance / patch testing. Irritant = cumulative or acute barrier damage, direct exposure reduction and barrier restoration.

Basic management in this lecture: reduce contact with irritants, use gentle cleansers, moisturizers and barrier creams; topical corticosteroids can be used to calm inflammation when appropriate.

6 · Atopic dermatitis: “the itch that rashes”

The lecturer emphasizes itch before rash: atopic patients scratch during sleep or with stress, perpetuating inflammation and chronic lichenification. Common associated history includes asthma, allergies and sensitive skin; extremes of temperature and humidity can exacerbate symptoms.

Infants / younger children

Prominent facial dermatitis.

Older children / adults

Typical flexural creases: antecubital and popliteal fossae.

Associated physical findings include infraorbital pleats and hyperlinear palms. Chronic scratch-rub cycles lead to lichenification.

Basic therapy

  • Avoid excessive temperature/humidity shifts and other personal triggers.
  • Gentle cleansers and soap substitutes; moisturizers emphasized as ointment > cream > lotion for moisturizing/occlusiveness.
  • Site-appropriate topical corticosteroids; nonsteroid topical calcineurin inhibitors pimecrolimus and tacrolimus.
  • Address sleep disruption, scratching and nail length; lecture references sedating antihistamines at bedtime.

Targeted inflammatory therapy

Agent/classTarget highlighted by lecture
DupilumabBlocks signaling from IL-4 and IL-13 (Th2 cytokines)
TralokinumabIL-13
NemolizumabIL-31 receptor
Topical / oral JAK inhibitorsSuppress signaling for multiple inflammatory cytokines
Slide safety reminders: biologic section mentions caution with live vaccines, noninfectious conjunctivitis and herpes reactivation; JAK inhibitors are associated with serious infection, malignancy, cardiovascular events and thromboses. Check agent-specific labeling rather than assigning every listed warning to every biologic.

Secondary infection recognition

Two high-yield patterns: Staphylococcus aureus impetiginized eczema versus herpes simplex eczema herpeticum, with grouped lesions. Herpeticum is a clinically significant complication requiring prompt recognition.

7 · Distinctive eczema patterns

Dyshidrotic eczema

Hand and foot eczema with deeply seated “tapioca pudding” vesicles, especially along the sides of fingers more than toes; may reach palms and soles. Lecture: strong topical steroid and gentle skin care.

Nummular eczema

Typically coin-shaped, subacute eczematous patches/plaques on arms and legs; lecturer lists a superpotent topical steroid.

Stasis dermatitis

Caused by venous insufficiency in the lower legs, producing dependent edema, erythema, scale, brown discoloration, and possible ulceration. Increased contact sensitization can complicate care, particularly to agents such as neomycin in triple-antibiotic ointment.

Therapeutic emphasis: manage leg edema with elevation/compression when appropriate; consider medication contributors listed in lecture (calcium channel blockers, gabapentin, pregabalin).

Asteatotic / xerotic eczema

Dry-skin eczema in older adults, swimmers and winter, worsened by frequent bathing and harsh soaps; slides also mention cholesterol-lowering agents. Eczema craquelé shows a cracked porcelain / dried riverbed appearance.

Habit-related forms

Lichen simplex chronicus: chronic focused rubbing/scratching causing a thickened plaque; lecturer illustrates superpotent topical steroid. Prurigo nodularis: recurrent picking producing nodules; lecturer notes increased risk with renal failure and options including intralesional corticosteroids, UV, nemolizumab or dupilumab.

DiagnosisMechanism / clueRecognize
Allergic contactType IV sensitizationNickel hardware/jewelry, poison ivy; delayed patch test
Irritant contactBarrier injurySoap/sanitizer, diaper moisture, saliva; no sensitization required
Atopic dermatitisIntense itch/atopic contextFace in infants; flexures later; chronic scratch changes
DyshidroticCharacteristic sites/vesiclesDeep “tapioca” vesicles on finger sides
NummularCharacteristic shapeCoin-shaped on limbs
StasisVenous hypertension / edemaLower legs, brown pigmentation, ulcers
AsteatoticXerosisWinter, older age, cracked porcelain
Lichen simplexRepeated rubbingLichenified plaque
Prurigo nodularisRepeated pickingFirm excoriated nodules
FOUNDATIONS LINK: Type IV allergy is T-cell mediated and delayed; spongiosis is extracellular fluid accumulating between keratinocytes, whereas acanthosis means increased epidermal thickness. This logic explains acute vesicles versus chronic thickening.

9 · Retrieval checkpoints

1. Acute vesicular eczema biopsy: what distinguishes it from chronic?

Acute = prominent spongiosis, intraepidermal vesicles, no acanthosis; chronic = hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen streaking.

2. Why can poison ivy continue after its vesicles rupture?

Blister fluid is not contagious; resin remains on contaminated nails, tools, clothes or animal fur. Delayed cell-mediated reactions and ongoing exposure explain new lesions.

3. Which exposure predicts allergic rather than irritant eczema?

Reproducible nickel eruption beneath jewelry or metal fastener in a previously sensitized person; confirm by patch testing when indicated.

4. Which is stronger: clobetasol 0.05% or hydrocortisone 2.5%?

Clobetasol 0.05%. Molecule and vehicle, not percentage alone, determine potency.

5. How does atopic dermatitis distribution change with age?

More facial in infants/young children; more antecubital and popliteal flexures in older children/adults.

6. Itchy deep vesicles along sides of fingers?

Dyshidrotic eczema (“tapioca pudding” vesicles).

7. Lower-leg edema, brown skin, scaling, venous ulcers?

Stasis dermatitis; recognize venous insufficiency and manage edema.

Master these before moving on

  1. Spongiosis / stage: Eczematous inflammation can go from vesicular/oosing acute lesions to chronic lichenification through itch–scratch loops.
  2. Allergic ≠ irritant: Memory T-cell type IV sensitization versus direct barrier damage.
  3. Topical steroid selection: Active molecule + vehicle + skin location; beware permanent striae and steroid-modified fungal infection.
  4. Atopic patterns: Distribution, itch and type 2 cytokine-targeted treatments.
  5. Subtype signature clues: Tapioca vesicles, coins, venous edema, cracked porcelain, repetitive rubbing versus picking.
